full_prose_under_review.title: Federal and Massachusetts Rule Interaction
learning_objectives: Solve a federal-state interaction by identifying the same actor, event, and prescription pathway under both sources.
Avoid selecting a familiar federal limit before checking Massachusetts conditions that also govern the transaction.

orientation.text: Two sovereigns reach the same dispensing at the same instant, and neither one announces where the other stops mattering. Federal controlled-substance regulation mostly draws an outer boundary: it describes the most a registrant may do without violating federal law. It does not confer authority to do that thing where the pharmacy actually stands. 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1) says so in its own text rather than leaving it to inference. The first condition of a patient-requested Schedule II partial fill is that the partial fill is NOT PROHIBITED BY STATE LAW, and the second is that the prescription is written and filled in accordance with the Act, that chapter, and State law. Federal permission therefore answers one question -- is this federally barred -- and expressly refers the rest back to the state. Read the wording exactly: the condition is an absence of state prohibition, not a requirement of affirmative state permission, so a jurisdiction that says nothing does not block the partial fill. A stricter Massachusetts rule is not in conflict with the federal permission either; it operates inside it, and it is the rule that decides what the pharmacist may actually do.

Put the two sources side by side on one transaction and the division of labour becomes visible. Federal law supplies the permission and the outer clock: a Schedule II prescription may be partially filled at the request of the patient, of someone acting on the patient's behalf, or of the practitioner who wrote it; the total dispensed across all partial fillings may not exceed the total prescribed; and any remaining portion, if filled, must be filled not later than 30 days after the date the prescription was written, or not later than 72 hours where the prescription was an emergency oral one. Massachusetts then supplies everything the federal rule leaves open. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) the pharmacist SHALL dispense the lesser quantity if the patient requests it, so what is permissive federally is compulsory here; only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion; and each partial dispensing and its quantity is noted in the pharmacy's patient record, accessible to the prescribing practitioner on request. Massachusetts states the same 30-day outer limit, measured from the prescription issue date, and adds a 5-day limit on the INITIAL partial dispensing that reaches only prescriptions filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), the two out-of-state pathways.

The second way the two sources interact is harder to see, because nothing about it looks like a conflict. Federal law and Massachusetts law each carry a five-refill limit and a six-month limit measured from the issue date, and the two numbers are identical. The scopes are not. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) is addressed to a controlled substance listed in Schedule III or IV: no such prescription may be filled or refilled more than six months after the date it was issued, and none authorised to be refilled may be refilled more than five times. 247 CMR 9.04(13) states the same two limits for Schedule V, and for Schedule V alone. Massachusetts then narrows its own provision by facility rather than by schedule: 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(13) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. Storing 'five refills, six months' as a single remembered fact loses all of this. The figure is correct in two places and controlling in neither until the schedule -- and, in Massachusetts, the facility -- is matched to the transaction in front of you.

A third pattern appears where one sovereign legislates and the other is simply silent. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) requires any prescription a practitioner issues for an opioid substance contained in Schedule II to include a notation on the prescription that the patient may fill it, upon request, in compliance with s. 18(d3/4), in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity. That duty has no federal counterpart, and it falls on the prescriber as a matter of what the prescription must contain. It is a different duty again from the pharmacy patient-record notation s. 18(d3/4) requires at each partial dispensing, and running the two together puts the obligation on the wrong actor. Silence on one side is not an argument that the transaction is unregulated. The working method that survives all three patterns is the same one: fix the schedule, the actor, the triggering event, the pathway and the facility before opening any rule, apply every rule whose scope actually reaches those facts, and read the stem for which sovereign it is asking about -- a stem that names a place rather than a body of law is asking about both.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient presents a Massachusetts-issued Schedule II opioid prescription for 60 tablets on the day it was written and asks for 20 tablets now. You dispense 20. Eighteen days later the patient asks a different pharmacy in the same chain for the remaining 40. That pharmacist checks 21 CFR 1306.13(b), sees that the remaining portion may be filled up to 30 days after the prescription was written, and prepares to dispense.
steps: Define the transaction before opening any rule: Schedule II, a Massachusetts-issued prescription filled in Massachusetts, a partial fill triggered by the patient's own request, and a remaining portion sought on day 18.

Federal law does reach these facts, and on the federal conditions alone the second pharmacist is right. The request came from the patient, the total across both fillings does not exceed the 60 tablets prescribed, and day 18 is inside the 30 days that run from the date the prescription was written.

But those same federal conditions make the partial fill contingent on its not being prohibited by State law and on the prescription being filled in accordance with State law. The federal rule points at Massachusetts rather than answering over it.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) provides that only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion. A different pharmacy, even one in the same chain, is not that pharmacy.

Test the 5-day figure before discarding it. It governs the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), the out-of-state pathways, and this prescription was not filled under either, so the figure never reaches these facts.
Close the record. The first pharmacy noted the partial fill and the quantity dispensed in the patient's record, and the remaining portion, when it is dispensed, generates the same notation there.
worked_examples.resolution: The second pharmacy may not dispense the remaining 40 tablets; the pharmacy that dispensed the first 20 must. The error the scenario invites is stopping at a federal permission that expressly refers the question back to State law. A second error sits alongside it: reaching for the 5-day figure, which belongs only to the s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) pathways and not to an ordinary in-state partial fill.

worked_examples.scenario: A Schedule V controlled-substance prescription written seven months ago, still showing two unused refills, is presented at a Massachusetts community pharmacy. A colleague reasons that 21 CFR 1306.22(a) states its six-month limit for Schedules III and IV only, that no federal six-month rule names Schedule V, and that the remaining refills may therefore be dispensed.
steps: The colleague has read the federal provision correctly. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) is addressed to a controlled substance listed in Schedule III or IV, and its six-month and five-refill limits are stated for those schedules.

Reading it correctly is not the same as finishing. A federal rule that does not reach Schedule V leaves the question open rather than resolving it in the pharmacy's favour, so the next step is to ask what Massachusetts says about the schedule in front of you.

247 CMR 9.04(13) supplies exactly the limits the federal provision does not: a Schedule V prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after the date it was issued, and may not be refilled more than five times.

Seven months have run from the issue date. The two unused refill authorisations do not survive that limit, because the six-month clock runs from issue rather than from the first or the most recent dispensing.

Confirm the facility before applying the Massachusetts provision. 247 CMR 9.04(15) removes 247 CMR 9.04(13) from institutional sterile compounding pharmacies; a community pharmacy is not one, so the provision reaches this dispensing.
worked_examples.resolution: No refill may be dispensed, and a new prescription is needed. The error the scenario invites is treating the absence of a federal rule as a permission, when the schedule the federal provision does not reach is precisely the one Massachusetts covers itself. The number the colleague needed was the same number he had already found, in the other sovereign's rule.

worked_examples.scenario: A Schedule II opioid prescription presented at your Massachusetts pharmacy carries no notation about partial filling. The patient asks you to dispense half of the prescribed quantity now. A technician tells you that because the prescription does not carry the notation the statute requires, the patient has no right to ask for a lesser quantity and you should dispense the full amount.
steps: Separate the two Massachusetts provisions the technician has run together. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) requires any prescription a practitioner issues for an opioid substance contained in Schedule II to include a notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in compliance with s. 18(d3/4), in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity.

Identify whose duty that is. The notation is a prescription-content duty owed by the prescribing practitioner. It is not a pharmacy recordkeeping step, and it is not stated as a condition on anything the patient may ask for.

The patient's entitlement sits elsewhere, in s. 18(d3/4): a pharmacist filling a Schedule II prescription shall, if requested by the patient, dispense the substance in a lesser quantity than the prescription indicates.

Federal law contributes only its outer conditions here, that the partial fill is not prohibited by State law, that the request came from the patient, and that the total dispensed across all partial fillings does not exceed the quantity prescribed.

Then complete the Massachusetts steps: note the partial dispensing and the quantity in the pharmacy's patient record, accessible to the prescribing practitioner on request, and keep the remaining portion at this pharmacy, to be filled not later than 30 days after the issue date.
worked_examples.resolution: Dispense the lesser quantity the patient requested. The error the scenario invites is converting a prescription-content duty that the statute places on the prescriber into a precondition of the patient's own right under s. 18(d3/4), and then into a ground for the pharmacist to refuse.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Fill in the blank: the first condition 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1) states for a patient-requested Schedule II partial fill is that the partial fill is ______. Why does the exact wording matter?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Not prohibited by State law. The condition is stated as an absence of state prohibition rather than as a requirement of affirmative state permission, so a jurisdiction that says nothing does not block the partial fill; restating it the other way reverses the default.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A patient partially filled a Schedule II prescription at pharmacy A and wants the remaining portion from pharmacy B on day 18. Which sovereign decides the point, and what is the answer?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Massachusetts decides. Federal law supplies the 30-day outer limit and does not address which pharmacy may dispense the remainder; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) allows only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity to dispense the remaining portion, so pharmacy B may not.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Fill in the blanks: the Massachusetts 5-day limit governs the ______ dispensing, and only where the prescription is filled pursuant to ______; the remaining portion must be filled not later than ______ after the prescription issue date.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Initial partial; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2); 30 days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the five-refill and six-month limits in 21 CFR 1306.22(a) are the source of the Massachusetts Schedule V refill limits.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) states those limits for Schedules III and IV. The identical Schedule V limits are Massachusetts law, at 247 CMR 9.04(13); matching numbers do not make the two provisions one rule.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which Massachusetts facility category does 247 CMR 9.04(13) not reach, and where is that stated?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(13), among others, do not apply to them, so a matching federal number does not remove the facility-scope inquiry.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which sovereign requires a Schedule II opioid prescription to carry a notation about the patient's partial-fill right, and on which actor does that duty fall?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Massachusetts, at M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c), and the duty falls on the prescribing practitioner as a matter of prescription content. It is not the pharmacy patient-record notation that s. 18(d3/4) separately requires at each partial dispensing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: where the s. 22(c) notation is missing from a Schedule II opioid prescription, the patient loses the right to request a lesser quantity.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The notation is a duty on the prescriber; the patient's right to a lesser quantity on request sits in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) and is not expressed as conditional on the notation appearing.

quick_review.text: Federal patient-requested Schedule II partial filling requires only that the partial fill not be prohibited by State law, alongside the other federal conditions in 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1).
Massachusetts supplies same-pharmacy, record, and issue-date requirements for its patient-requested Schedule II pathway.

Federal Schedule III-IV and Massachusetts Schedule V refill rules each use a five-refill limit and a six-month issue-date limit within their respective scope; Massachusetts excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(13).

decision_logic.condition: A transaction is governed by both federal and Massachusetts controlled-substance law.
decision_logic.action: Define the drug schedule, actor, trigger, and pathway first; then apply every rule whose scope actually reaches those facts.

decision_logic.condition: Federal law allows a patient-requested Schedule II partial fill that State law does not prohibit.
decision_logic.action: Continue to the Massachusetts conditions instead of stopping at federal permission.

decision_logic.condition: A refill question names Schedule III, IV, or Massachusetts Schedule V.
decision_logic.action: Choose the rule with the correct schedule scope, check both count and issue-date limits, and for the Massachusetts Schedule V rule confirm that the facility is not an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy.

ma_vs_federal.text: Federal permission for a patient-requested Schedule II partial fill does not displace Massachusetts' same-pharmacy and recordkeeping conditions, and Massachusetts additionally makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on patient request.

The similar five-refill and six-month formulations for Schedule III-IV and Massachusetts Schedule V must be matched to the correct schedule and facility scope; 247 CMR 9.04(13) does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

exceptions.text: A nearby rule with a familiar number is not controlling unless its actor, schedule, and triggering facts match the transaction.

Massachusetts excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from the Schedule V refill provision in 247 CMR 9.04(13), so the matching federal and state numbers do not eliminate the facility-scope inquiry.

The 30-day request-based remainder period is displaced by the federal 72-hour period for an emergency oral Schedule II prescription and is preceded by the Massachusetts five-day initial-dispensing limit for the s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) pathways.

timing_deadlines.consequence: Both federal and Massachusetts pathway limits must be satisfied.

timing_deadlines.consequence: The applicable five-refill limit must also remain unexhausted.

forms_records.text: The Massachusetts patient-requested Schedule II pathway requires a pharmacy patient-record notation for each partial dispensing and quantity.
A Massachusetts Schedule II opioid prescription must carry a notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity.

role_duties.duty: Apply federal permission and Massachusetts conditions to the same defined transaction before reaching a conclusion.

Transplanting a correct number from the wrong schedule produces a wrong result even when the number looks familiar.
Restating the federal not-prohibited-by-State-law condition as a requirement that State law affirmatively permit the partial fill changes the default for a silent jurisdiction.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Schedule II prescription may be partially filled at the patient or prescriber request when state law permits, with the remaining portion dispensed no later than 30 days after the prescription was written unless a shorter applicable limit controls.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws
authority.section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4), read with s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2)

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) a pharmacist filling a Schedule II prescription SHALL, if requested by the patient, dispense a lesser quantity; ONLY THE SAME PHARMACY that dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion; a notation of the partial fill and quantity goes in the patient record, accessible to the prescriber on request; and the remaining portion MUST BE FILLED NOT LATER THAN 30 DAYS AFTER THE PRESCRIPTION ISSUE DATE. The separate FIVE-DAY limit on the INITIAL partial dispensing applies only to a prescription FILLED PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (d) OR (d1/2) -- respectively a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription issued by an out-of-state practitioner, and a narcotic Schedule II prescription issued by a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth.
A Schedule III or IV prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after its issue date and may not be refilled more than five times unless renewed by the practitioner.
A Massachusetts Schedule V prescription may not be refilled more than five times or later than six months after the prescription was issued.

authority.name: Contents of prescription written by practitioner

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) any prescription issued by a practitioner for an OPIOID substance contained in Schedule II SHALL INCLUDE A NOTATION on the prescription that the patient may fill it, upon request, in compliance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) in an amount NOT TO EXCEED THE FULL PRESCRIBED QUANTITY. The notation is a prescription-content duty on the prescriber that accompanies the patient's statutory right to receive a lesser quantity on request.
exceptions: The notation duty reaches prescriptions for opioid substances in Schedule II; it is not a general notation requirement for every controlled-substance prescription.

full_prose_under_review.title: Schedule III-V Refills and Massachusetts Transfers
learning_objectives: Apply both the issue-date clock and refill-count limit to Schedule III and IV prescriptions.
Separate transfer eligibility from the prescription's remaining lawful refill capacity.
Recognize the special Massachusetts treatment of Schedule VI transfers.
Separate the federal one-time limit on a Schedule III-V refill transfer from the Massachusetts duty to transfer at the patient's request.
Identify who may execute a transfer, and separate the initial-dispensing electronic transfer from the refill-purpose transfer.

orientation.text: A refillable controlled prescription carries two separate ceilings, and both must be checked before every dispensing. One is a count of refills; the other is a clock that runs from the date the practitioner issued the prescription, not from the day the pharmacy first dispensed it. Federal law sets both for Schedules III and IV in a single sentence: no such prescription may be filled or refilled more than six months after the issue date, and no such prescription authorized to be refilled may be refilled more than five times. The word 'filled' matters. The six-month bar is not a limit on refills alone; a prescription that has never been dispensed at all is equally out of time once six months have passed. The two ceilings are also independent rather than cumulative, so a prescription with four unused refills and a seven-month-old issue date is exhausted, and a prescription two months old that has already been refilled five times is exhausted too. Neither ceiling is lifted by anything the pharmacy does; the practitioner must renew the therapy on a new prescription.

Massachusetts contributes the schedule the federal refill provision leaves out. 21 CFR 1306.22 is written for Schedules III and IV, and it does not supply refill limits for Schedule V. 247 CMR 9.04(13) fills that space with the same pair of numbers and the same structure: a licensee may not fill or refill a Schedule V prescription more than six months after the date it was issued, and a Schedule V prescription may not be refilled more than five times. Because the state provision borrows the federal shape, candidates often recall the figures correctly but attribute them to the wrong sovereign; on a Massachusetts Schedule V question the authority is the state regulation. That subsection also carries a facility-scope limit the federal rule has no counterpart to: 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(13) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. The exclusion removes that state subsection from that facility type; it does not disapply any other body of law that may reach the same dispensing.

Transfer is a different question from refill capacity, and confusing the two is the most productive error in this area. A transfer moves an existing prescription from one pharmacy to another. It does not create refill authority, and it does not restart the issue-date clock; the prescription arrives at the receiving pharmacy with exactly the refills and the issue date it already had. What Massachusetts adds is a duty on the pharmacy rather than a limit on the prescription. Under 247 CMR 9.14, a pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of a patient or the patient's agent, in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy; the pharmacy may act as the patient's agent in order to facilitate the transfer; and a pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription. That trio is a consumer-protection layer. It answers whether the pharmacy must move the prescription, who does the legwork, and what it may cost the patient. It says nothing at all about how many transfers the prescription itself is entitled to.

That second question is federal. 21 CFR 1306.25(a) permits the transfer of original prescription information for a Schedule III, IV or V controlled substance for the purpose of refill dispensing between pharmacies on a one-time basis only. The single circumstance that changes the number is a shared record: pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may instead transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization. The structure follows the concern. Each hand-off between two separate recordkeeping systems is a seam where a prescription could be dispensed twice, which is why the transferring pharmacist voids the original and the receiving pharmacist records where it came from and how many refills survive; where both pharmacies read and write the same live record, that seam does not exist and the cap is unnecessary. The two sovereigns then stack in one direction only. 21 CFR 1306.25(e) makes the federal procedure permissible only if allowable under existing State or other applicable law, so a state may withhold transfers the federal rule would permit. Nothing runs the other way: a state duty to transfer does not manufacture federal transfer capacity, so the Massachusetts obligation operates within the one-time cap rather than over it.

Massachusetts Schedule VI sits outside that federal cap entirely, and the reason is definitional. 105 CMR 700.002(F) provides that Schedule VI consists of all prescription drugs which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner, so a Schedule VI drug is by construction not a federally scheduled III, IV or V substance and 21 CFR 1306.25 never reaches it. The state regulation governs alone, and it is more generous than the federal rule it borrows its procedure from: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(a) directs that Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedules III through V prescriptions, 9.14(4)(b) permits transfer up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber, and 9.14(4)(c) supplies the only ceiling, barring transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date it was issued. Read those together and the Schedule VI limit is a count of refills bounded by an age, not a count of transfers. Note that the one-year figure in 9.14(4)(c) is a transfer bar, and this section's cited rules do not supply a Schedule VI refill ceiling of their own; do not import the five-refill and six-month figures from Schedules III through V into a Schedule VI prescription.

Finally, federal law offers two transfer pathways, not one, and they are told apart by whether the prescription has ever been dispensed. 21 CFR 1306.25 is the refill-purpose pathway just described: it presupposes a prescription with refills remaining, reaches Schedules III through V, and carries the shared-database allowance. 21 CFR 1306.08(e) is separate. It permits the transfer for initial dispensing of an electronic controlled-substance prescription between retail pharmacies, upon request from the patient, on a one-time basis only, and it reaches Schedules II through V. Where the prescription transferred on this pathway is a Schedule III, IV or V substance and includes authorized refills, those refills travel with the initial prescription to the receiving pharmacy. The pathway is narrow in the ways the refill-purpose rule is not: the prescription must stay in electronic form and must not be altered, and there is no shared-database counterpart, so it remains available once, whatever database the two pharmacies share. Both federal pathways require the transfer to be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, and both are permissible only where state law allows the transfer. That pharmacist-to-pharmacist requirement is why the Massachusetts allowance in 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) for a certified pharmacy technician to perform prescription transfers, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, is confined to Schedule VI, where no federal pathway operates.

worked_examples.scenario: A Schedule IV prescription was issued on 1 March authorizing five refills. The patient first had it dispensed on 5 March and used three refills at Pharmacy A. On 20 August she asks Pharmacy B to obtain it, and the transfer is completed on 22 August. On 10 September she asks Pharmacy B for the next refill. May Pharmacy B dispense it?
steps: Start with the two ceilings. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) bars filling or refilling a Schedule III or IV prescription more than six months after the date on which it was issued, so the window closes six months after 1 March.
Count the refills separately. Three of the five authorized refills have been used, so two remain and the five-refill ceiling is not the obstacle in this fact pattern.

Ask what the 22 August transfer changed. It moved the prescription without creating new refill authority and without restarting the issue-date clock, so the prescription reached Pharmacy B carrying the same 1 March issue date and the same two remaining refills.
Apply the clock on 10 September. The six-month period measured from 1 March has run, and unused authorized refills do not survive the time limit.
worked_examples.resolution: Pharmacy B may not dispense the refill; only a new prescription from the practitioner restores capacity. The scenario invites two errors at once: starting the six months at the 5 March first dispensing, and treating the two unused refills as authority that outlives the clock.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts patient's Schedule III prescription with refills remaining was transferred from Pharmacy A to Pharmacy B last month. She now asks Pharmacy C to obtain it from Pharmacy B, and mentions that Pharmacy B told her it would charge five dollars to send it and that she would have to telephone Pharmacy B herself. Pharmacies B and C do not share a prescription database.
steps: Identify the pathway. The prescription has already been dispensed and has refills remaining, so this is a refill-purpose transfer under 21 CFR 1306.25 rather than the initial-dispensing electronic transfer.

Apply the federal ceiling before the state duty. 1306.25(a) permits the refill-purpose transfer of Schedule III-V prescription information on a one-time basis only, and that transfer has already been used moving the prescription from A to B.

Test the exception. It is available only where the pharmacies electronically share a real-time, online database. B and C do not, so the alternative allowing transfer up to the maximum authorized refills is unavailable.

Do not read the Massachusetts duty as an override. 247 CMR 9.14(1) says when a pharmacy must transfer; 1306.25(e) makes the federal procedure permissible only if allowable under state law, so state law can withhold a federally permitted transfer but cannot supply federal transfer capacity the federal rule withholds.

Separate the two complaints the patient actually raised. The fee and the legwork are governed by 247 CMR 9.14(3) and 9.14(2), which forbid a transfer fee and permit the pharmacy to act as the patient's agent; those rules are unaffected by the transfer count.
worked_examples.resolution: The second refill-purpose transfer is not available on these facts, and a new prescription is what moves the therapy to Pharmacy C. The five-dollar charge and the instruction that the patient make her own telephone call were both improper regardless. The trap is reading the Massachusetts duty to transfer on request as removing the federal one-time cap.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts patient asks Pharmacy C to obtain a Schedule VI prescription issued eight months ago with four refills remaining. It has already been transferred once, from Pharmacy A to Pharmacy B. Pharmacy C has a certified pharmacy technician on shift and the pharmacist on duty approves her doing the work. A colleague objects that the federal one-time limit forbids a second transfer and that only a pharmacist may execute one.
steps: Classify the drug first. 105 CMR 700.002(F) makes Schedule VI all prescription drugs not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner, so this drug is not a federally scheduled III, IV or V substance.

That settles the first objection. 21 CFR 1306.25 governs the transfer of Schedule III, IV and V prescription information, so it never reaches this prescription and its one-time cap has nothing here to limit.

Apply the state rule that does govern. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(a) puts a Schedule VI transfer on the same footing as a Schedule III-V transfer, and 9.14(4)(b) permits transfer up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber, which is a count of refills rather than a count of transfers.

Check the state ceiling that does exist. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) bars transferring a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date it was issued, and eight months is inside that period.

Now the second objection. The federal requirement that a transfer be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists belongs to the federal pathways, which do not reach this prescription, and 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) permits a certified pharmacy technician to perform prescription transfers between pharmacies for Schedule VI only, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.
worked_examples.resolution: Both halves of the colleague's objection fail: the second transfer is permitted and the technician may execute it with the pharmacist's approval. The error the scenario invites is carrying a federal Schedule III-V mechanic across to a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription that no federal schedule reaches.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber transmits an electronic Schedule II prescription to retail Pharmacy A. The drug is out of stock and nothing has been dispensed. The patient asks Pharmacy A to send the prescription to retail Pharmacy B. A technician offers to print it and fax it across, and a colleague says a Schedule II prescription can never be moved between pharmacies.
steps: Rule out the wrong pathway. 21 CFR 1306.25 transfers prescription information for the purpose of refill dispensing, and this prescription has never been dispensed, so that rule is not the one in play.

Identify the right one. 21 CFR 1306.08(e) permits the transfer for initial dispensing of an electronic controlled-substance prescription between retail pharmacies, upon request from the patient, on a one-time basis only, and it reaches Schedules II through V.
Refuse the print-and-fax. The pathway requires the prescription to remain in electronic form and unaltered; converting it to another form defeats the transfer.

Refuse the technician's participation on this transfer. The federal pathway requires the transfer to be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, and the Massachusetts certified-technician transfer authority is confined to Schedule VI in any event.
Note what is not available here. This pathway carries no shared-database counterpart, so it stays one-time regardless of what record system the two pharmacies share.
worked_examples.resolution: The transfer is lawful, but only electronically, pharmacist to pharmacist, and once. The colleague's flat rule is the error the scenario invites; a never-dispensed electronic Schedule II prescription has a transfer pathway even though the refill-transfer rule does not reach Schedule II.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Schedule III or IV prescription may not be filled or refilled more than ______ after the date it was issued, and may not be refilled more than ______ times.
retrieval_prompts.answer: six months; five. Both limits are in 21 CFR 1306.22(a), and each is independent of the other.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which sovereign supplies the five-refill and six-month limits for a Schedule V prescription, and which facility type is excluded from them?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Massachusetts, at 247 CMR 9.04(13); the federal refill provision at 21 CFR 1306.22(a) is written for Schedules III and IV. 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that 9.04(13) does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the six-month clock starts running at the first dispensing, and it limits refills only.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False on both counts. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) and 247 CMR 9.04(13) each measure from the date the prescription was issued, and each bars filling as well as refilling once six months have passed, so a prescription that has never been dispensed is equally out of time.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How many times may Schedule III-V prescription information be transferred for refill purposes, and what single circumstance changes that number?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Once. Pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may instead transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A patient asks a retail pharmacy to move a never-dispensed electronic Schedule II prescription to another retail pharmacy. Which pathway applies, and does the shared-database allowance help?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The initial-dispensing electronic transfer under 21 CFR 1306.08(e), which reaches Schedules II through V. No: that pathway has no shared-database counterpart and stays one-time, and the prescription must remain electronic and unaltered.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: because Massachusetts requires a pharmacy to transfer on the patient's request, a Schedule IV prescription that has already been transferred once may be transferred again.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 247 CMR 9.14(1) says when a transfer must happen; 21 CFR 1306.25(a) says how many are available, and 1306.25(e) makes the federal procedure turn on state law permitting transfers rather than the reverse. Absent a shared real-time, online database, the second transfer is unavailable.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why does the federal one-time refill-transfer limit not cap a Massachusetts Schedule VI transfer, and what state ceiling applies instead?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because 105 CMR 700.002(F) makes Schedule VI all prescription drugs not included in any other schedule, so the drug is not a federally scheduled III, IV or V substance and 21 CFR 1306.25 never reaches it. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b) permits transfer up to the maximum remaining refills the prescriber authorized, and 9.14(4)(c) bars transfer of a refill-authorizing Schedule VI prescription more than one year after issue.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may execute a prescription transfer, federally and in Massachusetts?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Federally, the transfer must be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, on both the refill-purpose pathway and the initial-dispensing electronic pathway. Massachusetts adds that a certified pharmacy technician may perform prescription transfers between pharmacies for Schedule VI only, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

quick_review.text: Federal law bars filling or refilling a Schedule III or IV prescription more than six months after the issue date and bars more than five refills; only a new prescription lifts either limit.

For pharmacies subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13), a Massachusetts Schedule V prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after issue, and may not be refilled more than five times; that subsection does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.
Massachusetts requires a timely patient-requested transfer, prohibits a transfer fee, and permits a pharmacy to act as the patient's agent to obtain the transfer.

Transfer of Schedule III-V prescription information for refill purposes is permitted between pharmacies on a one-time basis only, unless the pharmacies electronically share a real-time, online database.

Transfer of an unfilled electronic controlled-substance prescription for initial dispensing is a separate federal pathway, permitted between retail pharmacies at the patient's request on a one-time basis only, and it reaches Schedules II through V.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule III or IV refill is requested.
decision_logic.action: Check both elapsed time from issue and the number of prior refills; either exhausted limit blocks the refill.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts Schedule V refill is requested at a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13).
decision_logic.action: Apply the five-refill and six-month limits independently.

decision_logic.condition: The facility is an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Do not apply the Schedule V refill limits in 247 CMR 9.04(13) through this provision; 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes that facility type.

decision_logic.condition: A patient or authorized agent requests a Massachusetts prescription transfer.
decision_logic.action: Transfer remaining authorized refills timely without charging a transfer fee, subject to the prescription-specific limits.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks to move a Schedule III, IV or V prescription with authorized refills remaining to another pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the prescription has not already been transferred once, unless the two pharmacies electronically share a real-time online database, before applying the Massachusetts transfer duty.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks a retail pharmacy to move an ELECTRONIC controlled-substance prescription that has never been dispensed to another retail pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Use the initial-dispensing electronic transfer pathway rather than the refill-transfer rule, keep the prescription in electronic form and unaltered, and treat it as available once only. A never-dispensed paper prescription has no federal transfer pathway.

ma_vs_federal.text: For Schedule III and IV refills the federal five-refill and six-month limits remain operative when the Massachusetts transfer rules are applied, and so does the separate federal limit permitting a Schedule III-V refill-purpose transfer only once.

Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions and may move up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, with the only ceiling being that a refill-authorising Schedule VI prescription may not be transferred more than one year after issue. The federal one-time limit does not cap them, because it reaches only federally scheduled III, IV and V substances and a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug is by definition in no other schedule.

A federal controlled-prescription transfer must pass directly between two licensed pharmacists, while Massachusetts lets a certified pharmacy technician do the work for Schedule VI only, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

exceptions.text: A transfer does not create new refill authority or restart an issue-date clock.
The Schedule V refill limits in 247 CMR 9.04(13) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies under 247 CMR 9.04(15).
Pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization instead of the one-time limit.
The real-time shared-database allowance belongs to the refill-purpose transfer rule; the initial-dispensing electronic transfer carries no such counterpart and stays one-time.

timing_deadlines.consequence: No further fill or refill after the federal time limit without practitioner renewal.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts Schedule V refill window at a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13)
timing_deadlines.consequence: No first fill and no refill after the state time limit, and no refill once five are used.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining-refill transfer of a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 1 year after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) does not permit that remaining-refill transfer after the one-year point.

role_duties.duty: Obtain the patient-requested transfer and preserve the remaining lawful refill limits.

Transfer the prescription at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay therapy, and complete the federal voiding and transfer records for a Schedule III-V refill transfer.
Communicate a federal controlled-prescription transfer directly between the two of them; the transfer is a pharmacist-to-pharmacist act.
Perform a prescription transfer only for Schedule VI, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

common_traps.text: Starting a six-month clock at the first dispensing rather than the issue date gives the prescription excess life.
Assuming a transfer renews or expands refill authority confuses movement of a prescription with creation of a new prescription.
Treating the Massachusetts duty to transfer on patient request as removing the federal one-time limit on a Schedule III-V refill transfer.
Concluding that a Schedule II prescription can never move between pharmacies overlooks the one-time initial-dispensing transfer of an unfilled electronic prescription.
Letting a certified pharmacy technician transfer a Schedule III-V prescription ignores both the Schedule VI limit on that authority and the federal pharmacist-to-pharmacist requirement.
Reading the Massachusetts Schedule V six-month limit as reaching only refills would let a seven-month-old prescription be dispensed for the first time.
Carrying the federal one-time transfer limit across to a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription refuses a second transfer the regulation allows.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Schedule III or IV prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after its issue date and may not be refilled more than five times unless renewed by the practitioner.

authority.name: Transfer between pharmacies of prescription information for Schedules III, IV, and V controlled substances for refill purposes

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Transfer of original prescription information for a controlled substance listed in Schedule III, IV or V for the purpose of refill dispensing is permissible between pharmacies ON A ONE-TIME BASIS ONLY; pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may instead transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization. The transfer must be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, the transferring pharmacist must void and annotate the original record, and the receiving pharmacist must record the required transfer data. The procedure is permissible only if allowable under existing State or other applicable law, and it moves the prescription without creating new refill authority or restarting the six-month issue-date clock.
exceptions: Pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization.
The transfer procedure is permissible only if allowable under existing State or other applicable law.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A Massachusetts Schedule V prescription may not be refilled more than five times or later than six months after the prescription was issued.

authority.name: Certified pharmacy technician Schedule VI transfer scope

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under current 247 CMR 9.14, a pharmacy must timely transfer a prescription at the request of the patient or authorized agent, may act as the patient's agent to obtain the transfer, and may not charge a transfer fee. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions; remaining authorized refills may be transferred, but a Schedule VI prescription may not be transferred more than one year after issuance. Under 247 CMR 8.04, a certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI transfer with approval of the pharmacist on duty.
exceptions: Schedule-specific federal requirements may add restrictions for federally controlled prescriptions; do not automatically import those mechanics into a Massachusetts Schedule VI transfer.

authority.name: One-time transfer of electronic controlled prescriptions

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: At a patient's request, an unfilled electronic Schedule II through V prescription may be transferred once between DEA-registered retail pharmacies if allowed by state law, kept electronic, unaltered, and communicated directly between pharmacists.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts Schedule VI includes prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Schedules I through V; Schedule VI status does not itself make a drug federally controlled or routinely MassPAT-reportable.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.
